A priest to whom the tenth lot came forth when David divided the priests ([1 Chr. 24:11](#1Chr.24.11)).
One of the priests who were set “to give to their brethren by courses” of the daily portion ([2 Chr. 31:15](#2Chr.31.15)).
A priest whose sons are mentioned in [1 Chr. 3:21](#1Chr.3.21), [22](#1Chr.3.22).
The father of Shemaiah, who repaired the wall of Jerusalem ([Neh. 3:29](#Neh.3.29)).
The son of Hamor the Hivite ([Gen. 33:19](#Gen.33.19); [34](#Gen.34)).
Father of one of those who accused Jeremiah to Zedekiah ([Jer. 37:3](#Jer.37.3); [38:1](#Jer.38.1)).
Father of a captain of the ward ([Jer. 37:13](#Jer.37.13)).

A name; renown, the first mentioned of the sons of Noah ([Gen. 5:32](#Gen.5.32); [6:10](#Gen.6.10)). He was probably the eldest of Noah’s sons. The words “brother of Japheth the elder” in [Gen. 10:21](#Gen.10.21) are more correctly rendered “the elder brother of Japheth,” as in the Revised Version. Shem’s name is generally mentioned first in the list of Noah’s sons. He and his wife were saved in the ark (7:13). Noah foretold his preeminence over Canaan (9:23-27). He died at the age of six hundred years, having been for many years contemporary with Abraham, according to the usual chronology. The Israelitish nation sprang from him ([Gen. 11:10-26](#Gen.11.10); [1 Chr. 1:24-27](#1Chr.1.24)).
One who stood by Ezra when he read the law ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
Rumour, a Benjamite whose sons “came to David to Ziklag” ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).
A prophet in the reign of Rehoboam ([1 Kings 12:22-24](#1Kgs.12.22)).
The eldest son of Obed-edom ([1 Chr. 26:4-8](#1Chr.26.4)).
A false prophet who opposed Jeremiah ([Jer. 29:24-32](#Jer.29.24)).
A Levite in the time of David, who with 200 of his brethren took part in the bringing up of the ark from Obed-edom to Hebron ([1 Chr. 15:8](#1Chr.15.8)).
One of the Levites whom Jehoshaphat appointed to teach the law ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).
A Levite appointed to “distribute the oblations of the Lord” ([2 Chr. 31:15](#2Chr.31.15)).
A false prophet who hindered the rebuilding of Jerusalem ([Neh. 6:10](#Neh.6.10)).
The father of Urijah the prophet ([Jer. 26:20](#Jer.26.20)).
The father of a prince in the reign of Jehoiakim ([Jer. 36:12](#Jer.36.12)).
One who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:5](#1Chr.12.5)).

Soaring on high, the king of Zeboiim, who joined with the other kings in casting off the yoke of Chedorlaomer. After having been reconquered by him, he was rescued by Abraham ([Gen. 14:2](#Gen.14.2)).
A Levite in David’s time ([1 Chr. 15:18](#1Chr.15.18), [20](#1Chr.15.20)).
A Levite in the reign of Jehoshaphat ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).
The son of Ammihud. He represented Simeon in the division of the land ([Num. 34:20](#Num.34.20)).
A prince of the tribe of Issachar ([1 Chr. 7:2](#1Chr.7.2)).
A Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:5](#1Chr.12.5)).
A Simeonite prince in David’s time ([1 Chr. 27:16](#1Chr.27.16)).
One of the princes who urged the putting of Jeremiah to death ([Jer. 38:1-4](#Jer.38.1)).
Root, a descendant of Manasseh ([1 Chr. 7:16](#1Chr.7.16)).
One of the messengers whom the children of the Captivity sent to Jerusalem “to pray for them before the Lord” ([Zech. 7:2](#Zech.7.2)).
A star, a prince at the court of Ahasuerus ([Esther 1:14](#Esth.1.14)).
Star of splendour, a Persian officer who vainly attempted to hinder the rebuilding of the temple ([Ezra 5:3](#Ezra.5.3), [6](#Ezra.5.6); 6:6, 13).
A Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 6:30](#1Chr.6.30)).
Another Levite of the family of Gershon ([1 Chr. 6:39](#1Chr.6.39)).
A Benjamite, a descendant of Gibeon ([1 Chr. 8:32](#1Chr.8.32)); called also Shimeam (9:38).

A Benjamite of the house of Saul, who stoned and cursed David when he reached Bahurim in his flight from Jerusalem on the occasion of the rebellion of Absalom ([2 Sam. 16:5-13](#2Sam.16.5)). After the defeat of Absalom he “came cringing to the king, humbly suing for pardon, bringing with him a thousand of his Benjamite tribesmen, and representing that he was heartily sorry for his crime, and had hurried the first of all the house of Israel to offer homage to the king” (19:16-23). David forgave him; but on his death-bed he gave Solomon special instructions regarding Shimei, of whose fidelity he seems to have been in doubt ([1 Kings 2:8](#1Kgs.2.8), [9](#1Kgs.2.9)). He was put to death at the command of Solomon, because he had violated his word by leaving Jerusalem and going to Gath to recover two of his servants who had escaped (36-46).
One of David’s mighty men who refused to acknowledge Adonijah as David’s successor ([1 Kings 1:8](#1Kgs.1.8)). He is probably the same person who is called elsewhere (4:18) “the son of Elah.”
A Levite of the family of Gershon ([1 Chr. 6:42](#1Chr.6.42)).
A son of Pedaiah, the brother of Zerubbabel ([1 Chr. 3:19](#1Chr.3.19)).
A Ramathite who was “over the vineyards” of David ([1 Chr. 27:27](#1Chr.27.27)).
One of the sons of Heman, who assisted in the purification of the temple ([2 Chr. 29:14](#2Chr.29.14)).
The father of one of the “valiant men” of David’s armies ([1 Chr. 11:45](#1Chr.11.45)).
Assisted at the purification of the temple in the time of Hezekiah ([2 Chr. 29:13](#2Chr.29.13)).
The mother of Jehozabad, who murdered Joash ([2 Kings 12:21](#2Kgs.12.21)); called also Shimrith, a Moabitess ([2 Chr. 24:26](#2Chr.24.26)).
Watchman, the fourth son of Issachar ([Gen. 46:13](#Gen.46.13); [1 Chr. 7:1](#1Chr.7.1); R.V., correctly, “Shimron”).

The shining one, or sunny, the secretary of Rehum the chancellor, who took part in opposing the rebuilding of the temple after the Captivity ([Ezra 4:8](#Ezra.4.8), [9](#Ezra.4.9), [17](#Ezra.4.17)-23).
Cooling, the king of Adamah, in the valley of Siddim, who with his confederates was conquered by Chedorlaomer ([Gen. 14:2](#Gen.14.2)).
Beauty, one of the Egyptian midwives ([Ex. 1:15](#Exod.1.15)).
Judicial, an Ephraimite prince at the time of the division of Canaan ([Num. 34:24](#Num.34.24)).

'=Sheshonk I., king of Egypt. His reign was one of great national success, and a record of his wars and conquests adorns the portico of what are called the “Bubastite kings” at Karnak, the ancient Thebes. Among these conquests is a record of that of Judea. In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign Shishak came up against the kingdom of Judah with a powerful army. He took the fenced cities and came to Jerusalem. …
One of David’s sons by Bathseheba ([2 Sam. 5:14](#2Sam.5.14)).
One of the sons of Caleb ([1 Chr. 2:18](#1Chr.2.18)), the son of Hezron.

Poured out, the “captain of the host of Hadarezer” when he mustered his vassals and tributaries from beyond “the river Euphrates” ([2 Sam. 10:15-18](#2Sam.10.15)); called also Shophach ([1 Chr. 19:16](#1Chr.19.16)).
The second son of Seir the Horite; one of the Horite “dukes” ([Gen. 36:20](#Gen.36.20)).
One of the sons of Caleb, and a descendant of Hur ([1 Chr. 2:50](#1Chr.2.50), [52](#1Chr.2.52); [4:1](#1Chr.4.1), [2](#1Chr.4.2)).
Captor, son of Nahash of Rabbah, the Ammonite. He showed kindness to David when he fled from Jerusalem to Mahanaim ([2 Sam. 17:27](#2Sam.17.27)).
A daughter of Heber the Asherite ([1 Chr. 7:32](#1Chr.7.32)).
A Canaanite whose daughter was married to Judah ([1 Chr. 2:3](#1Chr.2.3)).
One of Abraham’s sons by Keturah ([Gen. 25:2](#Gen.25.2); Chr. 1:32).
One of the descendants of Gershom, who had charge of the temple treasures in the time of David ([1 Chr. 23:16](#1Chr.23.16); [26:24](#1Chr.26.24)).
One of the sons of Heman; one of those whose duty it was to “lift up the horn” in the temple service ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4), [5](#1Chr.25.5)); called also Shubael (ver. 20).

The Lord sustains, one of David’s heroes ([1 Chr. 11:29](#1Chr.11.29)), general of the eighth division of the army (27:11). He slew the giant Saph in the battle of Gob ([2 Sam. 21:18](#2Sam.21.18); R.V., “Sibbechai”). Called also Mebunnai (23:27).

Striking down. The whole country on the east of Jordan, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, was possessed by the Amorites, whose king, Sihon, refused to permit the Israelites to pass through his territory, and put his army in array against them. The Israelites went forth against him to battle, and gained a complete victory. The Amorites were defeated; Sihon, his sons, and all his people were smitten with the sword, his walled towns were captured, and the entire country of the Amorites was taken possession of by the Israelites ([Num. 21:21-30](#Num.21.21); [Deut. 2:24-37](#Deut.2.24)).

Wood, a prominent member of the church at Jerusalem; also called Silvanus. He and Judas, surnamed Barsabas, were chosen by the church there to accompany Paul and Barnabas on their return to Antioch from the council of the apostles and elders ([Acts 15:22](#Acts.15.22)), as bearers of the decree adopted by the council. He assisted Paul there in his evangelistic labours, and was also chosen by him to be his companion on his second missionary tour ([Acts 16:19-24](#Acts.16.19)). He is referred to in the epistles under the name of Silvanus ([2 Cor. 1:19](#2Cor.1.19); [1 Thess. 1:1](#1Thess.1.1); [2 Thess. 1:1](#2Thess.1.1); [1 Pet. 5:12](#1Pet.5.12)). There is no record of the time or place of his death.

The second son of Jacob by Leah ([Gen. 29:33](#Gen.29.33)). He was associated with Levi in the terrible act of vengeance against Hamor and the Shechemites (34:25, 26). He was detained by Joseph in Egypt as a hostage (42:24). His father, when dying, pronounced a malediction against him (49:5-7). The words in the Authorized Version (49:6), “they digged down a wall,” ought to be, as correctly rendered in the Revised Version, “they houghed an ox.”
One of the ancestors of Joseph ([Luke 3:30](#Luke.3.30)).

Surnamed Niger, i.e., “black,” perhaps from his dark complexion, a teacher of some distinction in the church of Antioch ([Acts 13:1-3](#Acts.13.1)). It has been supposed that this was the Simon of Cyrene who bore Christ’s cross. Note the number of nationalities represented in the church at Antioch.

Originally called Simon (=Simeon, i.e., “hearing”), a very common Jewish name in the New Testament. He was the son of Jona ([Matt. 16:17](#Matt.16.17)). His mother is nowhere named in Scripture. He had a younger brother called Andrew, who first brought him to Jesus ([John 1:40-42](#John.1.40)). His native town was Bethsaida, on the western coast of the Sea of Galilee, to which also Philip belonged. Here he was brought up by the shores of the Sea of Galilee, and was trained to the occupation of a fisher. …

One of the twelve apostles, called the Canaanite ([Matt. 10:4](#Matt.10.4); [Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18)). This word “Canaanite” does not mean a native of Canaan, but is derived from the Syriac word Kanean or Kaneniah, which was the name of a Jewish sect. The Revised Version has “Cananaean;” marg., “or Zealot” He is also called “Zelotes” ([Luke 6:15](#Luke.6.15); [Acts 1:13](#Acts.1.13); R.V., “the Zealot”), because previous to his call to the apostleship he had been a member of the fanatical sect of the Zealots. There is no record regarding him.

A sorcerer of great repute for his magical arts among the Samaritans ([Acts 8:9-11](#Acts.8.9)). He afterwards became a professed convert to the faith under the preaching of Philip the deacon and evangelist (12, 13). His profession was, however, soon found to be hollow. His conduct called forth from Peter a stern rebuke (8:18-23). From this moment he disappears from the Church’s history. The term “Simony,” as denoting the purchase for money of spiritual offices, is derived from him.
A Christian at Joppa, a tanner by trade, with whom Peter on one occasion lodged ([Acts 9:43](#Acts.9.43)).

A Jew of Cyrene, in North Africa, then a province of Libya. A hundred thousand Jews from Palestine had been settled in this province by Ptolemy Soter (B.C. 323-285), where by this time they had greatly increased in number. They had a synagogue in Jerusalem for such of their number as went thither to the annual feasts. Simon was seized by the soldiers as the procession wended its way to the place of crucifixion as he was passing by, and the heavy cross which Christ from failing strength could no longer bear was laid on his shoulders. Perhaps they seized him because he showed sympathy with Jesus. He was the “father of Alexander and Rufus” ([Matt. 27:32](#Matt.27.32)). Possibly this Simon may have been one of the “men of Cyrene” who preached the word to the Greeks ([Acts 11:20](#Acts.11.20)).
One of the brothers of our Lord ([Matt. 13:55](#Matt.13.55); [Mark 6:3](#Mark.6.3)).
A leper of Bethany, in whose house Mary anointed our Lord’s head with ointment “as he sat at meat” ([Matt. 26:6-13](#Matt.26.6); [Mark 14:3-9](#Mark.14.3)).
Watchman, a Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 26:10](#1Chr.26.10)).
An inhabitant of Sin, near Arka ([Gen. 10:17](#Gen.10.17); [1 Chr. 1:15](#1Chr.1.15)).
Extension, the son of the giant whom Sibbechai slew ([2 Sam. 21:18](#2Sam.21.18)); called also Sippai ([1 Chr. 20:4](#1Chr.20.4)).

The captain of Jabin’s army ([Judg. 4:2](#Judg.4.2)), which was routed and destroyed by the army of Barak on the plain of Esdraelon. After all was lost he fled to the settlement of Heber the Kenite in the plain of Zaanaim. Jael, Heber’s wife, received him into her tent with apparent hospitality, and “gave him butter” (i.e., lebben, or curdled milk) “in a lordly dish.” Having drunk the refreshing beverage, he lay down, and soon sank into the sleep of the weary. …
The ancestor of some of the Nethinim who returned with Zerubbabel ([Ezra 2:53](#Ezra.2.53); [Neh. 7:55](#Neh.7.55)).

(Nubian, Sabako), an Ethiopian king who brought Egypt under his sway. He was bribed by Hoshea to help him against the Assyrian monarch Shalmaneser ([2 Kings 17:4](#2Kgs.17.4)). This was a return to the policy that had been successful in the reign of Jeroboam I.

Peaceful, (Heb. Shelomoh), David’s second son by Bathsheba, i.e., the first after their legal marriage ([2 Sam. 12](#2Sam.12)). He was probably born about B.C. 1035 ([1 Chr. 22:5](#1Chr.22.5); [29:1](#1Chr.29.1)). He succeeded his father on the throne in early manhood, probably about sixteen or eighteen years of age. Nathan, to whom his education was intrusted, called him Jedidiah, i.e., “beloved of the Lord” ([2 Sam. 12:24](#2Sam.12.24), [25](#2Sam.12.25)). He was the first king of Israel “born in the purple.” His father chose him as his successor, passing over the claims of his elder sons: “Assuredly Solomon my son shall reign after me.” His history is recorded in [1 Kings 1](#1Kgs.1)-11 and [2 Chr. 1](#2Chr.1)-9. His elevation to the throne took place before his father’s death, and was hastened on mainly by Nathan and Bathsheba, in consequence of the rebellion of Adonijah ([1 Kings 1:5-40](#1Kgs.1.5)). During his long reign of forty years the Hebrew monarchy gained its highest splendour. This period has well been called the “Augustan age” of the Jewish annals. The first half of his reign was, however, by far the brighter and more prosperous; the latter half was clouded by the idolatries into which he fell, mainly from his heathen intermarriages ([1 Kings 11:1-8](#1Kgs.11.1); [14:21](#1Kgs.14.21), [31](#1Kgs.14.31)).
The father who saves, probably the same as Sosipater, a kinsman of Paul ([Rom. 16:21](#Rom.16.21)), a Christian of the city of Berea who accompanied Paul into Asia ([Acts 20:4-6](#Acts.20.4)).

Safe in strength, the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, who was seized and beaten by the mob in the presence of Gallio, the Roman governor, when he refused to proceed against Paul at the instigation of the Jews ([Acts 18:12-17](#Acts.18.12)). The motives of this assault against Sosthenes are not recorded, nor is it mentioned whether it was made by Greeks or Romans. Some identify him, but without sufficient grounds, with one whom Paul calls “Sosthenes our brother,” a convert to the faith ([1 Cor. 1:1](#1Cor.1.1)).
Spike; an ear of corn, a convert at Rome whom Paul salutes ([Rom. 16:9](#Rom.16.9)).

Crown, a member of the church at Corinth, whose family were among those the apostle had baptized ([1 Cor. 1:16](#1Cor.1.16); [16:15](#1Cor.16.15), [17](#1Cor.16.17)). He has been supposed by some to have been the “jailer of Philippi” (comp. [Acts 16:33](#Acts.16.33)). The First Epistle to the Corinthians was written from Philippi some six years after the jailer’s conversion, and he was with the apostle there at that time.

One of the seven deacons, who became a preacher of the gospel. He was the first Christian martyr. His personal character and history are recorded in [Acts 6](#Acts.6). “He fell asleep” with a prayer for his persecutors on his lips (7:60). Devout men carried him to his grave (8:2).
Lily, with other pious women, ministered to Jesus ([Luke 8:3](#Luke.8.3)).
The father of Gaddi, who was one of the twelve spies ([Num. 13:11](#Num.13.11)).
Fortunate; affable, a female member of the church at Philippi, whom Paul beseeches to be of one mind with Euodias ([Phil. 4:2](#Phil.4.2), [3](#Phil.4.3)).
Impressions; rings, “the children of,” returned from the Captivity ([Ezra 2:43](#Ezra.2.43)).
Goodness of God, the father of one whom the kings of Syria and Samaria in vain attempted to place on the throne of Ahaz ([Isa. 7:6](#Isa.7.6)).
A Persian governor of Samaria, who joined others in the attempt to prevent the rebuilding of Jerusalem ([Ezra 4:7](#Ezra.4.7)).
Good is Rimmon, the father of Benhadad, king of Syria ([1 Kings 15:18](#1Kgs.15.18)).
The wife of Pharaoh, who gave her sister in marriage to Hadad the Edomite ([1 Kings 11:19](#1Kgs.11.19), [20](#1Kgs.11.20)).
One of the Anakim of Hebron, who were slain by the men of Judah under Caleb ([Num. 13:22](#Num.13.22); [Josh. 15:14](#Josh.15.14); [Judg. 1:10](#Judg.1.10)).

A king of Geshur, to whom Absalom fled after he had put Amnon to death ([2 Sam. 3:3](#2Sam.3.3); [13:37](#2Sam.13.37)). His daughter, Maachah, was one of David’s wives, and the mother of Absalom ([1 Chr. 3:2](#1Chr.3.2)).

A daughter of David ([2 Sam. 13:1-32](#2Sam.13.1); [1 Chr. 3:9](#1Chr.3.9)), whom Amnon shamefully outraged and afterwards “hated exceedingly,” thereby illustrating the law of human nature noticed even by the heathen, “Proprium humani ingenii est odisse quem laeseris”, i.e., “It is the property of human nature to hate one whom you have injured.”

The daughter-in-law of Judah, to whose eldest son, Er, she was married ([Gen. 38:6](#Gen.38.6)). After her husband’s death, she was married to Onan, his brother (8), and on his death, Judah promised to her that his third son, Shelah, would become her husband. This promise was not fulfilled, and hence Tamar’s revenge and Judah’s great guilt (38:12-30).
Consolation, a Netophathite; one of the captains who supported Gedaliah ([2 Kings 25:23](#2Kgs.25.23); [Jer. 40:8](#Jer.40.8)).
One of the “sons” of Javan ([Gen. 10:4](#Gen.10.4); [1 Chr. 1:7](#1Chr.1.7)).
One of Sennacherib’s messengers to Hezekiah ([2 Kings 18:17](#2Kgs.18.17)).

Gift, a Persian governor (Heb. pehah, i.e., “satrap;” modern “pasha”) “on this side the river”, i.e., of the whole tract on the west of the Euphrates. This Hebrew title pehah is given to governors of provinces generally. It is given to Nehemiah (5:14) and to Zerubbabel ([Hag. 1:1](#Hag.1.1)). It is sometimes translated “captain” ([1 Kings 20:24](#1Kgs.20.24); [Dan. 3:2](#Dan.3.2), [3](#Dan.3.3)), sometimes also “deputy” ([Esther 8:9](#Esth.8.9); [9:3](#Esth.9.3)). With others, Tatnai opposed the rebuilding of the temple ([Ezra 5:6](#Ezra.5.6)); but at the command of Darius, he assisted the Jews (6:1-13).
One of the sons of Ashur, the father of Tekoa ([1 Chr. 4:6](#1Chr.4.6)).

The wanderer; loiterer, for some unknown reason emigrated with his family from his native mountains in the north to the plains of Mesopotamia. He had three sons, Haran, Nahor, and Abraham, and one daughter, Sarah. …

Severe, a eunuch or chamberlain in the palace of Ahasuerus, who conspired with another to murder him. The plot was detected by Mordecai, and the conspirators were put to death ([Esther 2:21](#Esth.2.21); [6:2](#Esth.6.2)).

A modification of “Tertius;” a Roman advocate, whom the Jews employed to state their case against Paul in the presence of Felix ([Acts 24:1-9](#Acts.24.1)). The charges he adduced against the apostle were, “First, that he created disturbances among the Romans throughout the empire, an offence against the Roman government (crimen majestatis). Secondly, that he was a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes; disturbed the Jews in the exercise of their religion, guaranteed by the state; introduced new gods, a thing prohibited by the Romans. And thirdly, that he attempted to profane the temple, a crime which the Jews were permitted to punish.”
A badger, a son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother ([Gen. 22:24](#Gen.22.24)).

Lover of God, a Christian, probably a Roman, to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel ([Luke 1:3](#Luke.1.3)) and the Acts of the Apostles (1:1). Nothing beyond this is known of him. From the fact that Luke applies to him the title “most excellent”, the same title Paul uses in addressing Felix ([Acts 23:26](#Acts.23.26); [24:3](#Acts.24.3)) and Festus (26:25), it has been concluded that Theophilus was a person of rank, perhaps a Roman officer.

Thanksgiving, referred to by Gamaliel in his speech before the council at Jerusalem ([Acts 5:36](#Acts.5.36)). He headed an insurrection against the Roman authority. Beyond this nothing is known of him.

Twin, one of the twelve ([Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3); [Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18), etc.). He was also called Didymus ([John 11:16](#John.11.16); [20:24](#John.20.24)), which is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew name. All we know regarding him is recorded in the fourth Gospel ([John 11:15](#John.11.15), [16](#John.11.16); 14:4, 5; 20:24, 25, 26-29). From the circumstance that in the lists of the apostles he is always mentioned along with Matthew, who was the son of Alphaeus ([Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18)), and that these two are always followed by James, who was also the son of Alphaeus, it has been supposed that these three, Matthew, Thomas, and James, were brothers.

I.e., as known in Roman history, Tiberius Claudius Nero, only mentioned in [Luke 3:1](#Luke.3.1). He was the stepson of Augustus, whom he succeeded on the throne, A.D. 14. He was noted for his vicious and infamous life. In the fifteenth year of his reign John the Baptist entered on his public ministry, and under him also our Lord taught and suffered. He died A.D. 37. He is frequently referred to simply as “Caesar” ([Matt. 22:17](#Matt.22.17), [21](#Matt.22.21); [Mark 12:14](#Mark.12.14), [16](#Mark.12.16), [17](#Mark.12.17); [Luke 20:22](#Luke.20.22), [24](#Luke.20.24), [25](#Luke.20.25); 23:2; [John 19:12](#John.19.12), [15](#John.19.15)).

Building of Jehovah, the son of Ginath, a man of some position, whom a considerable number of the people chose as monarch. For the period of four years he contended for the throne with Omri ([1 Kings 16:21](#1Kgs.16.21), [22](#1Kgs.16.22)), who at length gained the mastery, and became sole monarch of Israel.

(in the LXX. called “Thorgal”), styled the “king of nations” ([Gen. 14:1-9](#Gen.14.1)). Mentioned as Tudkhula on Arioch’s brick (see facing page 139). Goyyim, translated “nations,” is the country called Gutium, east of Tigris and north of Elam.

An Assyrian king. It has been a question whether he was identical with Tiglath-pileser III. (q.v.), or was his predecessor. The weight of evidence is certainly in favour of their identity. Pul was the throne-name he bore in Babylonia as king of Babylon, and Tiglath-pileser the throne-name he bore as king of Assyria. He was the founder of what is called the second Assyrian empire. He consolidated and organized his conquests on a large scale. He subdued Northern Syria and Hamath, and the kings of Syria rendered him homage and paid him tribute. His ambition was to found in Western Asia a kingdom which should embrace the whole civilized world, having Nineveh as its centre. …
Defiled, the father of blind Bartimaeus ([Mark 10:46](#Mark.10.46)).
Honouring, one of the seven deacons at Jerusalem ([Acts 6:5](#Acts.6.5)). Nothing further is known of him.
Honouring God, a young disciple who was Paul’s companion in many of his journeyings. …
The youngest of the sons of Japheth ([Gen. 10:2](#Gen.10.2); [1 Chr. 1:5](#1Chr.1.5)).

The last king of Egypt of the Ethiopian (the fifteenth) dynasty. He was the brother-in-law of So (q.v.). He probably ascended the throne about B.C. 692, having been previously king of Ethiopia ([2 Kings 19:9](#2Kgs.19.9); [Isa. 37:9](#Isa.37.9)), which with Egypt now formed one nation. He was a great warrior, and but little is known of him. The Assyrian armies under Esarhaddon, and again under Assur-bani-pal, invaded Egypt and defeated Tirhakah, who afterwards retired into Ethiopia, where he died, after reigning twenty-six years.
The youngest of Zelophehad’s five daughters ([Num. 26:33](#Num.26.33); [Josh. 17:3](#Josh.17.3)).

Honourable, was with Paul and Barnabas at Antioch, and accompanied them to the council at Jerusalem ([Gal. 2:1-3](#Gal.2.1); [Acts 15:2](#Acts.15.2)), although his name nowhere occurs in the Acts of the Apostles. He appears to have been a Gentile, and to have been chiefly engaged in ministering to Gentiles; for Paul sternly refused to have him circumcised, inasmuch as in his case the cause of gospel liberty was at stake. …
